directions.name: Food safety & quality
directions.day: You check that food is made safely and that the rules are followed. You walk through kitchens or production lines, take samples, keep records and explain what needs to change.
directions.where: Food factories, catering companies, supermarket suppliers and hotel groups.
directions.bring: Six years in restaurant kitchens, where food safety rules apply every day.
directions.know: Many of these jobs ask for a higher food safety certificate than kitchen staff need. Some employers pay for the course.

directions.name: Buying & suppliers
directions.day: You decide what a company buys, compare prices, talk to suppliers and make sure the right ingredients arrive on time.
directions.where: Food wholesalers, restaurant groups, catering companies and food factories.
directions.bring: You said you enjoy ordering stock and dealing with suppliers. That is this job on a small scale.
directions.know: Most of the day is at a desk, on the phone and in spreadsheets. Search for “assistant buyer” first, because “buyer” on its own often means several years of experience.

directions.name: Production planning
directions.day: In a large kitchen or food factory, you plan what gets made each day, how much, and by whom. When an order changes, you sort out the plan.
directions.where: Food factories, bakeries, central kitchens of restaurant chains and airline caterers.
directions.bring: Six years of kitchen services, each one a plan that has to come together at a fixed time.
directions.know: Factories often run early shifts. If daytime hours matter to you, check the hours in each ad.

directions.name: Recipe & product development
directions.day: You invent and test new dishes or products for a food company or a chain, write the recipes down exactly, and adjust them until they work in large amounts.
directions.where: Food manufacturers, supermarket suppliers and restaurant chains.
directions.bring: Your training as a chef and six years of cooking. This is the direction closest to the cooking itself.
directions.know: These jobs are fewer than the others, and many sit in food factories that supply supermarkets. They usually have office hours.

directions.name: Teaching & training
directions.day: You teach cooking at a college, in a training kitchen or to new staff. You plan sessions, show techniques and help people get better.
directions.where: Colleges, cookery schools, training companies and large restaurant groups.
directions.bring: You said you like showing new cooks how things work. That is most of this job.
directions.know: College jobs may ask for a teaching certificate, which can often be done part-time while you work.

directions.name: Sales & customer care for food suppliers
directions.day: You look after restaurants and shops that buy from a food supplier. You visit them, take orders, suggest products and fix problems.
directions.where: Food wholesalers, drinks companies, equipment suppliers and specialist food producers.
directions.bring: You’ve been on the other side: you said you order stock and deal with suppliers in your kitchen.
directions.know: Sales jobs usually come with targets. Customer care jobs look after customers you already have. Check which one an ad really describes.

directions.name: Cooking in schools, hospitals & care homes
directions.day: You still cook, but in daytime hours. You plan menus for people with different needs, such as allergies or soft diets, and run a small team.
directions.where: School caterers, hospitals, care homes and councils.
directions.bring: Your six years of cooking, and these jobs mostly have the daytime hours you said you want.
directions.know: Pay is often by the hour, and school jobs may be term time only. Work out the yearly total before comparing.

options: Reworking tomorrow’s production plan after a big order came in late
Showing a group of trainees how to break down a whole chicken
Visiting a restaurant that buys from us to talk through its new menu
Cooking lunch for a school, with three different allergy versions

questions.q: Which finished piece of work would make you proudest?
options: A kitchen that passed its inspection because of the changes I suggested
A new sauce on supermarket shelves, made from my recipe
A customer who stayed with us for years because I looked after them
A care home menu that the residents look forward to

questions.q: How much contact with people do you want in a working day?
options: Some, mostly short visits and talks about what I found
Lots of calls and emails with suppliers, from a desk
A room full of people for most of the day
A small team I know well, and the people we cook for

questions.q: A delivery arrives with half the order missing. What do you want to do?
options: Check whether what did arrive is safe to use
Call the supplier and get the rest here this afternoon
Rework today’s plan around what we actually have
Tell our customers early and offer them something else

questions.q: Which part of a new menu would you want to work on?
options: Finding suppliers and a good price for the ingredients
Working out how to make it in large amounts, on time
Creating and testing the dishes until they’re right
Making sure everyone can eat it, including special diets

questions.q: Which compliment would mean the most to you?
options: “Everything was ready on time, as always.”
“You explained it so that I finally got it.”

questions.q: Every job has some pressure. Which kind could you live with?
options: Prices going up, and having to find a cheaper way
A launch date for a product that isn’t right yet
A class that isn’t getting it, with an exam coming
A monthly target that shows clearly how I’m doing

questions.q: How would you like your week to look?
options: At a desk most days, with the odd visit to a supplier
A timetable of sessions that repeats every week
On the road, visiting different customers each day
Monday to Friday, and home by mid-afternoon

questions.q: Think of a good day in a kitchen. What made it good?
questions.hint: Any good day counts, even a small one.
options: Everything was clean, labelled and in its place
A huge service went exactly to plan
A regular came back to tell us how much they loved it
I cooked something simple that made someone’s day

questions.q: A café wants to throw away less food. Which part is yours?
options: Checking how food is stored and how long it really lasts
Ordering smaller amounts, more often, from the right suppliers
Creating dishes that use up what’s left over
Planning portions so people get what they need, no more

questions.q: Someone hands you a messy stock room. What do you most want to do?
options: Throw out what’s past its date and label everything else
Count it all and fix what we order next time
Plan the week’s cooking around what’s already there
Show the team a system so it stays tidy
I like comparing options until I find the right deal
I like it when a plan works out exactly
I like trying something new to see if it works
I like it when I can win someone over

questions.q: What gives you energy at work?
options: Ticking off a long list and seeing things get done
Seeing someone get better at something week by week
Knowing that what I cooked really mattered to someone

questions.q: A food company gives you one month. Which task do you pick?
options: Write clear food safety instructions for all their kitchens
Create a new vegetarian range for their shops
Plan and run the training for their new kitchen staff
Win five new restaurants as customers
